title: Merge K Sorted Lists
statement: You are given an array of k linked lists, each already sorted in ascending order. Merge them into one sorted linked list and return its head.
realWorld: This is the merge phase of every external sort and every LSM-tree compaction: k sorted runs on disk, far more data than fits in memory, and a single sorted output stream. Databases, log-structured stores and MapReduce shuffles all run exactly this loop, with a heap of k file cursors.

examples.explanation: Both 1s appear; a merge preserves duplicates. The output is the multiset union in sorted order.
No lists at all — return null, not an empty node.
One list, which is empty. The array is non-empty but every entry is null, so the heap never receives anything.

constraints: The total number of nodes across all lists will not exceed 10^4

bruteForce.idea: Merge the lists one at a time: fold list 1 into list 0, then list 2 into that result, and so on.
code: merged = mergeTwo(merged, list);   // re-walks everything merged so far
private static ListNode mergeTwo(ListNode a, ListNode b) {
ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0), tail = dummy;
if (a.val <= b.val) { tail.next = a; a = a.next; }

complexity.time: O(k·N) where N is the total number of nodes

bruteForce.whySlow: The accumulated result is walked again on every merge. After i merges it holds roughly i·N/k nodes, and merging list i+1 into it touches all of them, so the total is N/k · (1 + 2 + … + k) = N(k+1)/2 — quadratic in k. The nodes of the first list are re-read k times even though they never move relative to each other. With k = 10,000 that is 10,000 passes over data that was already in order.

patternIdentification: At every step the question is identical: of the k list heads still standing, which is smallest? That is 'repeatedly take the current extreme from a changing set', which is the defining heap signal. The set changes by exactly one element per step — one head is consumed, its successor takes its place — so you want a structure that supports remove-min and insert in O(log k), not one that re-scans all k heads. Note the size bound: the heap holds one node per *list*, never one per element, so it is O(k) space regardless of how long the lists are.

optimized.idea: Put the head of every non-empty list into a min-heap ordered by node value — at most k nodes. Repeatedly poll the smallest, append it to the output, and if the node it came from has a successor, offer that successor. The heap therefore always holds exactly the current front of each list still in play. Every node is offered once and polled once, and each of those operations is O(log k) because the heap never exceeds k entries.
code: /** O(N log k) time, O(k) space. N = total nodes, k = number of lists. */
if (head != null) heap.offer(head);      // skip empty lists — null breaks the comparator
ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0);            // removes the 'is this the first node?' branch
heap.offer(smallest.next);           // that list's new front, O(log k)
tail.next = null;                            // sever any stale link from the last node

complexity.space: O(k) for the heap; O(1) extra beyond it, since nodes are relinked rather than copied

heap[size++] = head.val;                           // seed: the front of each list
int i = size - 1;                                  // sift up from the new leaf
while (i > 0 && heap[(i - 1) / 2] > heap[i]) {     // parent bigger? property broken
swap(heap, i, (i - 1) / 2);                    // swap with the parent
i = (i - 1) / 2;                               // climb; i == 0 is the root
int min = heap[0];                                 // poll: the next output value
heap[0] = heap[--size];                            // last leaf fills the hole at the root
int j = 0, c;                                      // sift down from the root
while ((c = smallerChild(heap, j, size)) != j) { swap(heap, j, c); j = c; }
// then offer smallest.next — the same list's new front — and repeat

commonMistakes: Offering null heads. `Comparator.comparingInt(node -> node.val)` throws a NullPointerException the moment a null enters the heap, and an empty list in the input array is a null head. Filter them when seeding.

Putting every node of every list into the heap up front. That is O(N log N) time and O(N) space — you have written heapsort. The heap must hold one node per list, which is the entire reason the bound is log k and not log N.
Forgetting to offer `smallest.next` after polling, which silently truncates every list to its first element.
Not severing `tail.next` at the end. The last node still points into its original list, so the result can contain a stale tail or, if lists were built from a shared pool, a cycle.

Comparing with `(a, b) -> a.val - b.val`. Fine for the stated constraints, wrong in general: the subtraction overflows for values far apart, giving a comparator that is not transitive and a heap that returns wrong answers. `Comparator.comparingInt` costs nothing extra.
Handling `lists = null`, `lists = []` and `lists = [null]` as if they were the same as a normal input — each must return null without touching the heap.

Missing the alternative the interviewer usually asks for: divide and conquer, pairing the lists up and merging pairs until one remains. Also O(N log k) — log k rounds, each touching all N nodes — with O(1) extra space and better cache behaviour, but O(log k) recursion depth.
